newsitem.title: PERU: Peru crisis negotiations resume after week's break.
newsitem.headline: Peru crisis negotiations resume after week's break.

text.p: Talks between the Peruvian government and Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home were set to resume later on Wednesday, a member of the talks guarantors commission said.
"This afternoon, talks start again," Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani told reporters.

Cipriani delivered the single-phrase statement after he and two other guarantors -- Canadian ambassador Anthony Vincent and Michel Minnig of the Red Cross -- met rebel leader Nestor Cerpa inside the besieged residence for an hour and 20 minutes earlier on Wednesday.
Cipriani and Vincent also met with government negotiator Domingo Palermo on Tuesday in an effort to persuade the sides back to the negotiating table for the first time in a week.

Talks to end the siege peacefully seemed to be progressing steadily until the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels broke off face-to-face meetings on Thursday and charged the government with planning to take the building by storm through a secret tunnel.

After energetic meetings with both sides, the guarantors arranged a for a fresh round of talks on Monday, only to have the government call off the meeting, accusing the rebels of trying to backtrack on the progress already made.

The siege began on Dec. 17 when the rebels blasted into a cocktail party hosted by the Japanese ambassador and took all the guests hostage. The rebels released most of them in the first few days, but kept some as bargaining chips, including Fujimori's brother Pedro, two of his cabinet ministers, the Japanese ambassador and a long list of Japanese businessmen.

The 72 men held by the MRTA, who are demanding freedom for some 400 jailed comrades, are basically in good health but are showing growing signs of chronic stress, including gum disease and skin ailments, after 85 days in captivity, said a doctor who is a member of a Red Cross team treating them.
"They are showing problems common to people in captivity, complications related to chronic angst," the doctor, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters.
The plight of the hostages, holed up inside the mansion with the windows closed and no air conditioning during the hot Lima summer, has drawn more attention in Peru as the talks sputtered.

Local television said one of the hostages, Bolivian Ambassador Jorge Gumucio, had "an attack of hysteria" and calmed down only after being shouted at by a rebel. Several doctors have been seen walking into the residence in recent days.
The doctor said he had seen about 14 cases of inflamed gums, which causes serious tooth pain, and other dental ailments caused or aggravated by long-term stress, he said.

A few hostages have developed a skin disease that causes flaking on the arms and uncontrollable itching, the doctor said. He personally treated one such case but had heard of others, plus one case of unusual hair loss and another of psoriasis -- all associated with stress.

"We know these people were healthy when they came because they were all taken captive at a party, and you don't go to a party if you're sick," the doctor said. "The important thing is that all these ailments are being treated."
The captives seemed to be in generally good spirits and he had not seen cases of depression, he said. "The hostages are all talented people with great human qualities."
Fujimori said he would exhaust all peaceful means to end the siege but hinted again at his refusal to rule out force if the guerrillas harmed the hostages in any way.

"I repeat and I insist that we will always exhaust all the peaceful measures at our disposal and we hope that the same contact is maintained -- that is to say, that there are no victims inside," Fujimori told reporters on Tuesday.
